# A lattice-preserving normal form for a positive cap circuit

Consider k ambient halfspaces

`H_i={v_i.z+u_i.x>=b_i}`,

where the continuous normals u_i form a minimal positive dependence: there
are lambda_i>0 with `sum lambda_i u_i=0`, and no proper subfamily admits a
positive dependence. Then k<=d+1 and their rank is k-1.

Rescale each inequality by lambda_i and write u_i',v_i',b_i'. Put

`vbar=(1/k)sum v_i'`, `bbar=(1/k)sum b_i'`.

The only linear dependence among the u_i' is their sum. Consequently there
exist a linear map A:R^n->R^d and y in R^d satisfying

`u_i'.A=v_i'-vbar`, `u_i'.y=b_i'-bbar` for every i.

Under the fiber shear `x'=x+A z-y`, every inequality becomes

`u_i'.x'+ell(z)>=0`, where `ell(z)=vbar.z-bbar`.

This transformation fixes all integer coordinates and translates every
continuous fiber, preserving the mixed lattice, mixed volume, and the full
ambient halfspace family exactly.

Proof of the rank assertion: if the kernel of the matrix of continuous
normals had dimension at least two, an independent kernel vector could be
added to the strictly positive dependence until some coordinate first became
zero while the others remained nonnegative. This would produce a positive
dependence on a proper subfamily. Thus rank=k-1 and k<=d+1. The stated linear
systems are solvable because their right sides have the same unique relation.

The open caps cover the whole continuous fiber exactly when ell(z)>0. For
ell(z)=0 the closed caps cover it, but their open versions miss the common
nullspace of the continuous normals. For ell(z)<0, x'=0 is missed even by the
closed caps. When k=d+1, the intersection of the caps for ell(z)>0 is a
homothetic simplex, of scale ell(z).

## Exact obstruction to a tempting circuit-mass inequality

It is FALSE that a single positive circuit of d+1 caps covering every fiber
in an integer halfspace must contain one cap with at least gamma_d times the
covered mixed volume. Different parity classes can support different
exclusive cap colors, even when the circuit covers all of R^(n+d).

Here is an exact n=d=2 example. Let Q be the standard integer triangle with
vertices z_1=(0,0), z_2=(1,0), z_3=(0,1). These are its only integer points.
Let

`p_1=(3,-1)`, `p_2=(-1,3)`, `p_3=(-1,-1)`,
`D=[-1/10,1/10]^2`, `K_i=p_i+D`,
`C=conv(union_i {z_i} x K_i)`.

The set C is a full-dimensional convex body in R^4, since it is a fiber shear
of Q x D. Its mixed-integer set has exactly the three indicated fibers, of
common area V=1/25. Consider the three caps

`H_1={x_1>=-1/10}`,
`H_2={x_2>=-1/10}`,
`H_3={-x_1-x_2>=-1/10}`.

Their continuous normals sum to zero, and their open versions cover all of
R^4: the sum of their three defining margins is 3/10. Each cap contains
exactly its own fiber K_i and misses the other two, with strict margins.
Thus each cap has mixed mass V=M/3, less than gamma_2 M=4M/9.

This example has three different integer parity classes. Any successful use
of the circuit normal form must therefore couple its continuous geometry to
a genuine allocation of parity costs. Counting circuits alone is insufficient.
